Two New Species Of The Genus Anolis From Hispaniola And Puerto Rico.
Anoles are a group of lizards that have been studied for decades by herpetologists and evolutionary biologists alike because they provide an excellent model system to study speciation in action as well as other aspects of evolution such as adaptation or phenotypic plasticity. In this paper we describe two new species from Hispanola and one from Puerto Rico based on morphological characters including coloration patterns but also using molecular data which allowed us to confirm their distinctiveness at both genetic level and morphology. We found these three taxa were genetically isolated with respect to each others suggesting strong reproductive isolation between them despite being geographically close together. This is important information when considering conservation efforts aimed towards preserving biodiversity within islands like Cuba where many endemic lizard genera exist yet there has not been much research done about how closely related some populations may be compared to those living elsewhere even if only separated by small distances across island chains.
The authors conclude:
"Given our results it seems likely that further investigation into the phylogeography of Cuban anole will reveal more cryptic diversity than currently recognized."

Two New Species Of The Genus Anolis From Hispaniola And Puerto Rico.
Anoles are a group of lizards that have been studied for decades by herpetologists and evolutionary biologists alike because they provide an excellent model system to study speciation in action as well as other aspects of evolution such as adaptation or phenotypic plasticity. In this paper we describe two new species from Hispanola and one from Puerto Rico based on morphological characters including coloration patterns but also using molecular data which allowed us to confirm their distinctiveness at both genetic level and morphology. We found these three taxa were genetically isolated with respect to each others suggesting strong reproductive isolation between them despite being geographically close together. This is important information when considering conservation efforts aimed towards preserving biodiversity within islands like Cuba where many endemic lizard genera exist yet there has not been much research done about how closely related some populations may be compared to those living elsewhere even if only separated by small distances across island chains.
The authors conclude:
"Given our results it seems likely that further investigation into the phylogeography of Cuban anole will reveal more cryptic diversity than currently recognized."

A new way to Make Solar Cells - 2012-08-30, by ANS (http://www.ans.org/)
The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

A new way to Make Solar Cells - 2012-08-30, by ANS (http://www.ans.org/)
The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

A new way to Make Solar Cells - 2012-08-30, by ANS (http://www.ans.org/)
The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

A new way to Make Solar Cells - 2012-08-30, by ANS (http://www.ans.org/)
The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

A new way to Make Solar Cells - 2012-08-30, by ANS (http://www.ans.org/)
The University of New South Wales has developed a method for making thin-film silicon-based photovoltaic devices that is much cheaper and more efficient than current methods.
In the journal Nature Photonics this week, UNSW researchers describe how they have used an inexpensive chemical process called electrochemical deposition to create high-quality crystalline silicon films on glass or plastic substrates at room temperature in just minutes using low-cost materials such as sodium silicate solution and copper foil electrodes.
This technique could be scaled up easily so it would become possible to manufacture large-area flexible PV modules with very good efficiency – potentially even better than today’s rigid single-crystal Si wafers.
“Electrodeposition can produce highly uniform layers over wide areas,” says Professor Martin Green from UNSW's Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics . “It also allows us to use cheap raw material solutions like Na _{4} SiO _{3} , which are readily available.”
Professor Green said his team had been working towards developing electrodeposited polycrystalline silicon since he first demonstrated its potential back in 2005 when he was still based at the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory .
“We’ve now shown we’re able to deposit continuous monocrystalline-like silicon ribbons directly onto any substrate without having to grow them into separate crystals then cut them apart later," Professsor Green explains.
“This means you don’t need expensive equipment to do crystal growth; instead all your processing steps take place after growing the film."
He adds: "We believe our approach will lead to significant cost reductions because there won't be many different processes involved compared to conventional manufacturing techniques where each step requires specialised tools costing tens if not hundreds of thousands dollars."

cat is a common sight in the streets of Tokyo. But this one has an unusual ability: it can see infrared light, which humans cannot detect.
The feline was found by researchers at Japan's National Institute for Materials Science (NIMS) to have special cells that are sensitive to heat radiation from 8-14 microns wavelength - invisible wavelengths beyond red but within human vision range.
This means cats like her may be able to spot warm-blooded prey such as mice or birds even when they're camouflaged against their surroundings.
"Such animals would not only help us understand how other species perceive thermal information," said Naoaki Yoshida who led research on the animal published online Wednesday in Nature Communications journal."But we also hope our findings will lead to new technologies."
Yoshida explained his team had been studying "heat-sensing proteins", known as thermoreceptors, since 2009 after discovering them in some insects living near hot springs.
They were looking into whether these receptors could work with mammalian eyesight systems because many mammals use both visual and olfactory cues to find food sources.
Infrared-sensitive neurons called rods exist inside all vertebrate retinas except those belonging to primates including people.
However scientists believe there might still be room left over in primate brains where more specialised sensors could operate alongside existing ones.
To test if any remained available, Japanese researcher used genetic engineering techniques to insert genes coding for insect-like thermosensitive protein opsins into mouse embryos before implanting them back into female hosts.
After birth, offspring developed two types of photopigment molecules capable of detecting visible blue-green light while retaining sensitivity towards longer-wavelengths than usual.
When tested using standard laboratory equipment, results showed the modified rodents' rod-shaped sensory organs responded strongly to far-infrared rays between eight-and-a-half-to-nine-micrometres long.
"This suggests that the newly created opsin-based receptor system functions similarly to natural thermo-receptor mechanisms present in most non-primates," wrote authors.
"The discovery opens up possibilities for developing novel optoelectronic devices based upon biological components".

When connected together, both sets of data allow researchers to work out what part of the animal's mind corresponds exactly to its body parts. By doing this repeatedly during training sessions, animals learn to associate certain mental images with physical actions. Then when asked to perform tasks mentally but not physically, say walking forwards while sitting still, the same neural pathways fire off automatically.
